books.section: Topic 4.9 The Development of an American Culture, B. European Romanticism and American Culture

stimulus.text: In the early 1800s many Americans loved the novels of the British writer Sir Walter Scott. His Ivanhoe, set in twelfth-century England, was full of castles, knights, and heroic figures. American writers admired Scott's romantic spirit — its feeling, imagination, and love of a colorful past — but they set their own stories in American places: forests, frontiers, and small towns.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.9 B: Americans were captivated by Scott's novels, with classical historical settings (Ivanhoe was set in twelfth-century England) and larger-than-life heroic figures, and American authors then created literature that drew on Scott's romanticism but was distinctly American. Original synthesis, not a quotation.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: American romantic writers differed from Scott mainly in that they did which of the following?

options.text: Refused to write novels at all
options.misconception: Cooper and Irving wrote stories and novels, so it is easy to misremember their forms.

options.text: Wrote only about the cities of Europe
options.misconception: Scott set books in Europe, so it is easy to think his admirers did the same.

options.text: Ignored nature and the past entirely
options.misconception: American writers look practical, so it is easy to think they skipped nature and the past.

options.text: Romantic feeling in American settings: wilderness, not castles

rationales.A: Cooper's Leatherstocking Tales are novels, and Irving's stories filled books; they wrote plenty of fiction.
rationales.B: The stimulus says American writers set stories in American places, not in European cities.
rationales.C: Nature and the past are exactly what Cooper and Irving wrote about, in forests and old Dutch towns.
rationales.D: Scott gave them the feeling; America gave them the scenery — frontier forests in place of medieval castles.
rationales.general:
1. Hold the two halves of the stimulus apart. Scott's spirit on one side, American places on the other.
2. Ask what changed in the crossing. The castles stayed in England; the forests and frontiers took their place.
Background: the United States lacked ancient ruins, so its painters and writers turned to pristine wilderness.
Remember: influence is not imitation — look for what the borrower changed.
